title: [inductor] Multiple randint calls cause inconsistent RNG results between eager and compiled mode after fixing the rng seed
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug To reproduce: ```python import torch import torch._dynamo torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True def fn(): torch.manual_seed(0) out = torch.randint(0, 100, (4,1), dtype=torch.int64) # Shape and integer range are not important. other = torch.randint(0, 100, (2,1), dtype=torch.int64) # No inconsistency if remove this line, although the value won't be returned. return out cfunc = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor') torch.manual_seed(0) out1 = fn() torch.manual_seed(0) out2 = cfunc() print(f'{out1=}') ''' out1=tensor([[44], [39], [33], [60]]) ''' print(f'{out2=}') ''' out2=tensor([[33], [60], [63], [79]]) ''' torch.testing.assert_close(out1, out2, equal_nan=True) ``` Problem: RNG state is inconsistent between eager execution and torch.compile(backend='inductor') execution, even after explicitly resetting the seed with torch.manual_seed(0) before each run. The issue occurs when two randint calls are called inside the compiled function:the output of the first randint already differs between eager and compiled mode, even though the second randint result is not returned. After a few debugging, I notice that the following version does NOT trigger the inconsistency: ```python def fn(): torch.manual_seed(0) out = torch.randint(0, 100, (4,1), dtype=torch.int64) torch.manual_seed(0) # Extra seed reset before second randint other = torch.randint(0, 100, (2,1), dtype=torch.int64) return out ``` The only difference is an extra torch.manual_seed(0) before the second randint. This behavior is bit counterintuitive: We already set the seed before the first `randint`, and the second `randint` does not modify the returned value. However, without setting the second `randint`'s rng seed still causes the first randint output to mismatch between eager and compi...
comments_excerpt: Reproduced with Inductor only. Not sure if this counts as silent incorrectness, so flagging for triage review. I've opened a draft PR with a proposed fix: [https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/176842](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/176842) The change prevents RNG ops (such as `aten.randint`) from being reordered in `reorder_for_locality`, which can otherwise lead to inconsistent RNG results between eager and compiled execution. I would appreciate a response.

title: CUDA target overloads not handling kwargs
issue_body_excerpt: <!-- Thanks for opening an issue! To help the Numba team handle your information efficiently, please first ensure that there is no other issue present that already describes the issue you have (search at https://github.com/numba/numba/issues?&q=is%3Aissue). --> ## Reporting a bug <!-- Before submitting a bug report please ensure that you can check off these boxes: --> - [x] I have tried using the latest released version of Numba (most recent is visible in the change log (https://github.com/numba/numba/blob/main/CHANGE_LOG). - [x] I have included a self contained code sample to reproduce the problem. i.e. it's possible to run as 'python bug.py'. This: ```python import numpy as np from numba.cuda import jit from numba.extending import overload def bar(): pass @overload(bar, target='cuda') def ol_bar(x, kw1=None): def impl(x, kw1=None): return 123 return impl @jit def foo(arr): arr[0] = bar(2) tmp = np.zeros((1,)) foo[1, 1](tmp) print(tmp) ``` Fails typing with `TypeError("Signature mismatch: 1 argument types given, but function takes 2 arguments")`.
comments_excerpt: The issue seems to be that kwargs aren't considered when producing the args for compilation, this patch seems to fix it: ```diff diff --git a/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py b/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py --- a/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py +++ b/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py @@ -763,6 +763,7 @@ class CUDADispatcher(Dispatcher, serialize.ReduceMixin): # Ensure an exactly-matching overload is available if we can # compile. We proceed with the typing even if we can't compile # because we may be able to force a cast on the caller side. + pysig, args = self._compiler.fold_argument_types(args, kws) if self._can_compile: self.compile_device(tuple(args)) ``` cf. `_DispatcherBase` https://github.com/numba/numba/blob/f4b6fe0124fa7734ba2bb28c7685db5b6306c486/numba/core/dispatcher.py#L359 Notes from triage meeting: - There was a PR that attempted to add kwargs to CUDA, but I wasn't in support of the approach there, because it deviates from the core kwargs mechanism (#7871) - The above patch makes it look like argument folding works, but IIRC it will be incorrect if kwargs are in a different order in the parameter list to those in the declaration. I had an experiment with folding args (using a slightly different method to enable it) in https://github.com/gmarkall/numba/commit/1db1c44be1a541e73269ba12131762891d8410f5 Given that it is hard to make it work in general and maintain parity with the core dispatcher, we probably want to prevent kwargs being used for CUDA overloads. Some additional notes from an OOB discussion. The above one-line patch in https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/8528#issuecomment-1286983427 would potentially "fix" the use of `kwargs` when calling from device to device. Some investigation is needed into whether this is indeed the case.

title: Support For CPU Atomics
issue_body_excerpt: ## Feature request It would be great if there were a way to use atomic operations from within numba. Currently atomic operations are only supported when generating cuda or HSA code. I'm currently experimenting with using numba to write callbacks that are provided to a C++ concurrency library. In this context, atomics are useful in that they can reduce the amount of synchronization required (or to write the locks that are actually being used). You can technically use atomic operations now if you hide them inside a function pointer exported from C++, but the performance impacts of doing so aren't clear to me. At first glance, preventing inlining seems like a high price to pay for every atomic operation. With regards to what would be the most useful, weak memory consistency is by far the most common thing that shows up in the applications I'm looking at right now, but what's needed is application specific in general. Other consistencies could potentially be useful to me for being able to acquire/release existing locks without having to route everything through an externally compiled function, but that's more of a secondary concern at the moment.
comments_excerpt: FYI I was just looking at this and you can achieve it reasonably with https://gist.github.com/sklam/40f25167351832fe55b64232785d036d (renamed to `numba.extending.intrinsics`), but it requires a bit of llvm work. Neat example! I hadn't seen that before. To document a use case for this feature: the [HogWild! algorithm](http://papers.nips.cc/paper/4390-hogwild-a-lock-free-approach-to-parallelizing-stochastic-gradient-descent) requires atomic floating-point addition. While that may be achievable in Numba's CUDA support, we need atomic intrinsics (ideally applicable to NumPy arrays, an intrinsic atomic `arr[i] += x` operation) in order to make such implementations that work without a GPU. Just wanted to add to this, I’ve felt a need for this when I wanted to: * generate large histograms in parallel (too large to give each thread a copy) * perform GraphBLAS-like parallel graph computations Yep, my use-cases involve parallel graph analytics as well. Adding another request for CPU atomics. I'm not sure how multi-dimensional cases are handled, but abstractly if there was an `atomic_add(arr, indx, val)` `atomic_compare_and_swap(arr, index, expected, new)` and an `atomig_get(arr, index)` that would be enough for me to work around a lack of other operations and get stuff working. This would let me get some [n-gram based](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00200) parallel computing working and be enough for a lot of common workloads like Hogwild. voting up! Something like CUDA's atomicAdd, atomicMin, etc would be helpful. For the OMP hackend, the ``#pragma omp atomic`` should be of some help? I attempted to write an atomic add using `@intrinsic` about it is held up by https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/6920.

comments_excerpt: I believe it's not a bug. Try: ` X_block_ptr = tl.advance(X_block_ptr, (block_size, 0))` I am already using that. ``` for _ in range(0, M, block_size): x = tl.load(X_block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1), padding_option="zero") s = tl.sum(x, axis=0) s = tl.sum(s, axis=0) acc += s tl.advance(X_block_ptr, (block_size, 0)) ``` To clarify, `tl.advance` doesn't have side effects, you need to assign the return value to block_ptr. That fixed it! Thanks :-)

title: torch.compile: autograd.Function.apply with aliased inputs drops per-slot gradient contributions
github_labels: high priority|triaged|module: correctness (silent)|oncall: pt2|module: dynamo|module: higher order operators|module: pt2-dispatcher|dynamo-autograd-function|pt2: ubn|bot-triaged
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug When the same Tensor is passed to two (or more) positional tensor arguments of a `torch.autograd.Function.apply(...)`, and the backward returns different values for those positions (e.g. `None` for one slot and a tensor for another), `torch.compile` produces a graph that drops one of the per-slot gradient contributions. In eager, autograd accumulates both slot contributions into a single `.grad` on the shared input. Under `torch.compile`, dynamo collapses the aliased inputs to a single HOP argument and then maps backward returns incorrectly — only one of the duplicated slots' return values ends up as the gradient for the deduped input. cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @amjames @Lucaskabela @jataylo @azahed98 @ydwu4 @bdhirsh @bobrenjc93 @anijain2305 @xmfan — related to the area you worked on in #180642 / #180670 / #180921, but the mechanism here is input aliasing rather than fwd side-effects, and it survives those fixes on current `main`. ### Minimal repro (~50 LOC, pure PyTorch, no triton, no custom ops) ```python import torch class MyFn(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, q, k, v, mask_v_grad: bool): ctx.save_for_backward(q, k, v) ctx.mask_v_grad = mask_v_grad return q * (k + v) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, dout): q, k, v = ctx.saved_tensors dq = dout * (k + v) dk = dout * q dv = dout * q if ctx.mask_v_grad: dk = dk + dv # bwd pre-aggregates; returns None for v slot return dq, dk, None, None return dq, dk, dv, None def f(q, k): return MyFn.apply(q, k, k, True).sum() # same tensor k at slots 2 AND 3 device = "cuda" for label, g in [("eager", f), ("compile", torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True))]...
comments_excerpt: I reproduced the bug on current main. The root cause is in `AutogradFunctionApplyVariable.rewire_bwd_graph_outputs` in `torch/_dynamo/variables/higher_order_ops.py`, when the same tensor is passed to multiple positional slots of `apply()`, the loop over `orig_fwd_args` blindly overwrites `outer_fwd_proxy_to_bwd_node[fwd_proxy]` on each iteration instead of accumulating, so only the last slot's backward contribution survives. Fix: extract `fwd_proxy = fwd_arg.proxy` and accumulate via `bwd_graph.call_function(operator.add, ...)` when the proxy is already mapped to a non-None node, and guard the None assignment with `if fwd_proxy not in outer_fwd_proxy_to_bwd_node` to prevent None from overwriting a real gradient. All 8 permutations of the 3-alias case pass, and the full `AutogradFunctionTests` suite passes with no regressions. Happy to submit a PR for this if that would be helpful. I just wanted to check before opening one. I also think this can be solved by accumulating the per-slot backward returns for deduplicated inputs, which would follow eager mode's `InputBuffer::add` behavior. Happy to submit a PR!

title: Return a view from tensor(requires_grad=False) in autograd function may cause incorrect requires_grad attribute.
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ```python import torch a = torch.rand(4, requires_grad=True) b = a.view(4) assert b.requires_grad and b._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): c = b.view(4) assert c.requires_grad class View(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x): # return x.data.view(x.shape) return x.detach().view(x.shape) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, grad): return grad d = View.apply(a) assert d.requires_grad and d._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): e = d.view(4) assert e.requires_grad # AssertionError ``` The variable `d` in the `forward` method of other `autograd.Function` implementations may behave differently compared to `b`. But I don’t have any method to distinguish between them. ### Versions Versions of relevant libraries: [pip3] numpy==2.3.4 [pip3] nvidia-cublas-cu12==12.6.4.1 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-cupti-cu12==12.6.80 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-nvrtc-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] nvidia-cudnn-cu12==9.10.2.21 [pip3] nvidia-cufft-cu12==11.3.0.4 [pip3] nvidia-curand-cu12==10.3.7.77 [pip3] nvidia-cusolver-cu12==11.7.1.2 [pip3] nvidia-cusparse-cu12==12.5.4.2 [pip3] nvidia-cusparselt-cu12==0.7.1 [pip3] nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.27.5 [pip3] nvidia-nvjitlink-cu12==12.6.85 [pip3] nvidia-nvtx-cu12==12.6.77 [pip3] pytorch-triton==3.5.0+git7416ffcb [pip3] torch==2.10.0.dev20251023+cu126 [pip3] torchvision==0.25.0.dev20251023+cu126 cc @ezyang @albanD @gqchen @nikitaved @soulitzer @Varal7 @xmfan
comments_excerpt: You should not use `.data` in general. If you want to detach from the autograd graph, you can use `.detach()` But within a custom Function forward, since autograd is already disabled, you can just do return `x.view(x.shape)` @albanD Using `.detach()` can also reproduce this issue, while `x.view(x.shape)` seems to resolve it. title: `snt_check()` appears not to handle core count correctly

comments_excerpt: Hi @nyck33, can you please include an example of the errors you're facing? I'm going to do my best to guess what might be going wrong. Another user recently reported this error: ``` ImportError: libcudart.so.11.0: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory ``` RAPIDS is currently built on CUDA 11, so you need to install a CUDA Toolkit with that major version. Note that it's fine to use a newer _driver_ but the system must have a CUDA 11 _toolkit_. If this is the error you see, I think there is room for improvement in the docs. Both WSL2 support and pip support are fairly new, so we appreciate your help in reporting this. I'll file a PR to clarify this requirement in the docs here: https://docs.rapids.ai/install#pip-install In the meantime, I think you have a couple options: - Install a `cuda-toolkit` package inside WSL that is major version 11 (I recommend 11.8, the most recent minor version of CUDA 11). You can get that from this link: https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-11-8-0-download-archive?target_os=Linux&target_arch=x86_64&Distribution=WSL-Ubuntu&target_version=2.0&target_type=deb_network - Note that you want to install `cuda-toolkit` and _not_ `cuda`, because `cuda` will include a driver as well as the toolkit. WSL can have problems if you install a driver package in WSL, because that driver should come from the host Windows machine. This is discussed further here: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/wsl-user-guide/index.html#cuda-support-for-wsl-2 - Install via conda. Installations with conda will come with `cudatoolkit` from `conda-forge`, and that means you don't have to install the CUDA Toolkit into your WSL system. @bdice that is exactly the problem I was facing but I went ahead and tried to fix it and that error disappeared but I'll try as you say...

title: poly1d with int64 arrays -- unexpected output
issue_body_excerpt: ### Description Hi there, I've found unexpected behaviour when fitting a polynomial using an int64 array. It seems that a polynomial created with `p = cp.poly1d(cp.polyfit(x, y, N))` requires a float array `x` when calling via `p(x)` -- see code example below. The output of `cp.polyfit` looks the same so `poly1d` seems to be the culprit. The key point is how to evaluate the performance impact of configurations in an efficient way. @jerrychenhf , are you proposing adding new device-capabilities-aware filters to filter out configurations? Say - Step 1: Keep the current configuration logic to produce configurations - Step 2: Apply filters to the produced configurations for performance Is my understanding correct? @EikanWang > are you proposing adding new device-capabilities-aware filters to filter out configurations? Yes > * Step 1: Keep the current configuration logic to produce configurations > * Step 2: Apply filters to the produced configurations for performance Step 1: Exactly yes. Step 2: Apply filters to reduce "OBVIOUS BAD" config based on device capabilities, grid and per cta work information. Will NOT try to figure out new config which might be more performant than the current ones. Figuring out and add more config will be always part of Step 1. Step 1: focus to getting enough configs to autotune. It may have two types of configs: **A**. General configs added only considering the type of kernel like pointwise, reduction, etc **B**. More performant configs added by considering the problem shape, device capabilities, etc Step 2: do a reduce of configs based on some simple principles regarding the device capabilities, grid and per cta work information. This is major for simplify the Step 1 - **A** type of configs since we can add generally more configs without very careful checking. So even we have Step 2 (remove known worst configs waste time to benchmark). It is still valuable in Step 1 to add **B** type of configs (figure to include best configs in search space).

issue_body_excerpt: Claude-generated description of the issue and repro: ``` """Minimal repro: cudf-polars streaming-mode broadcast bug for `with_columns(pl.lit(<numpy_array>))` at >~1M rows. comments_excerpt: Pinned memory is for the host memory allocation. Please check https://docs.cupy.dev/en/stable/user_guide/memory.html for details. I think the point here is that the pinned memory can also be safely used directly from the GPU. So it's legitimate to want to wrap up the pinned pointer into a cp.ndarray. This function works: ``` def from_numpy_pinned(x: np.ndarray, order='C') -> cp.ndarray: assert order in 'FC' # TODO: support K memptr = cupy.cuda.alloc_pinned_memory(x.nbytes) memptr_ndarray = np.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, buffer=memptr, order=order) memptr_ndarray[:] = x # cupy rejects this simple approach (https://github.com/cupy/cupy/issues/8697): #return cupy.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, memptr=memptr, order=order) # We instead have to treat the memory as unowned to sneak it into a cupy array mem_unowned = cupy.cuda.UnownedMemory(ptr=memptr.mem.ptr, size=memptr.mem.size, device_id=cupy.cuda.runtime.getDevice(), owner=memptr.mem) memptr_unowned = cupy.cuda.MemoryPointer(mem_unowned, offset=0) return cupy.ndarray(x.shape, dtype=x.dtype, memptr=memptr_unowned, order=order) ``` I think this avoids leaking the memory because `memptr.mem` is a `cupy.cuda.pinned_memory.PinnedMemory` object, which has. `__del__` method that deallocates the pinned memory.

comments_excerpt: Thanks for the report - will look into this shortly! I can reproduce the issue - marking as a bug. I think this will be tricky to fix - it seems like the gufunc broadcasting mechanism is limited to adding axes, and the kernel implementation assumes that the broadcasted array will be contiguous. I had a try in a branch to fix up the broadcasting, but my solution implemented broadcasting with zero strides, in the same way that NumPy does (see https://github.com/gmarkall/numba/commit/ae96876cb29242699bfb904c2614300a3b9922f8). This gets the shapes and strides of inputs and outputs right for this example, but the result is rubbish because the distribution of elements to threads was incorrect. It seems like there would be quite a lot of work to rewrite things more generally to support this use case - however, pinging @sklam for a second opinion. Note: this works fine on the CPU because Numba only has to compile the gufunc there, and NumPy takes care of broadcasting. @gmarkall, the note on broadcasted array has to be contiguous is correct. The emitted kernel is expecting the outer-dims (looped-over axes) are flattened so it can do a 1-D kernel configuration. I tried a hack to make sure the outer-dims are flatten in a 1-D loop and it seems to work for this case. issue_body_excerpt: While the current ability to pass a dict of dtypes to `rtol=` and `atol=` is nice, in practice it is used pretty rarely meaning that double precision routines are often tested with the same precision as single precision ones. comments_excerpt: Repro with triton commit: af76c989eb4799b015f8b288ccd8421558772e56 cc @jansel I don't think it's technically a bug. The auto-tuner will just run all the configs one by one and see which one is fastest. In this case, you have: ``` tmp7 = tl.load(in_out_ptr0 + (r2 + (384*x3)), xmask & rmask, eviction_policy='evict_last') ... tl.store(in_out_ptr0 + (r2 + (384*x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, RBLOCK], tl.int32)), tmp19, xmask & rmask) ``` so when the kernel runs twice, the first call modifies `in_out_ptr0` which leads to the wrong value being loaded in the second call. The same issue arised when doing `atomic_add` in a matmul with SPLIT_K>1, and we fixed the issue by adding a hook in the auto-tuner that resets the desired arguments to zeros between runs: https://github.com/openai/triton-mlir/blob/main/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L25-L33 I imagine in your case we'd want the hook to initialize data from a copy. Re-tagging this as an enhancement as we probably want to revisit the autotuner API and document this behavior properly. I don't think it'll be possible to have a general analysis pass that determines which arguments should be copied upfront -- this would work in simple cases but likely would fail when aliasing behavior is dynamic. Ah I think you are correct. The autotuner runs the kernel multiple times, which is not safe to do for in-place kernels because the first run clobbers the input data. comments_excerpt: cc @grlee77 Thanks for reporting this @PCRedHot. I suspect this is related to integer overflow. In the example code above, it looks like `data_array_cupyx` is cast from `uint8` to `int8` via `astype`, but this wasn't done in the SciPy case? title: RFC: Separate NumPy and CPython implementions/functionality.
issue_body_excerpt: This is an RFC on altering Numba's fundamental numerical functionality to better reflect what is present in Python/NumPy. The intended impact of this is to: * Ensure better reproducibility, i.e. Numba will more closely follow what would happen in the interpreter. * Alter performance characteristics with an anticipated net performance gain. * Create conceptually easier paths to follow to achieve higher performance. **Current state:** At present, the Numba code base implements a large number of the functions found in Python builtins, Python's `operator`, `math` and `cmath` modules, and NumPy. Due to historical reasons (largely from the way in which the compiler was bootstrapped) a lot of the implementations of the functions are reasonable approximations for "common" input values that are in use by most users, but they often fail to replicate functionality _exactly_. This "reasonable approximation" has served Numba well, but the current state has a few fundamental problems: 1. The functions often call into each others' implementations, for example NumPy `ufuncs` that "borrow" implementation details from the `math` module. The performance characteristics can be somewhat unpredictable due to this as the implementations from Python modules often contain exception handling whereas NumPy does not. Exceptions lead to branches which lead to lost optimisation opportunities in e.g. vectorization. 2. The implementations are sufficiently acceptable along "common" paths, but are often not correctly implemented with respect to things like type promotion or error handling. 3. title: [Feature request] Vulkan Target
issue_body_excerpt: I was trying different python parallelization/jit frameworks like jax and taichi, but I am always coming back to Numba due to it being beginner friendly and one can gradually increase the efficiency with further understanding. With that being said, I was a bit sad to see that only CUDA was supported as a GPU backend (now it is managed with a [plugin by nvidia](https://github.com/NVIDIA/numba-cuda) themselves) while the support for AMD (ROCm) was first added and then removed. Supporting all of the platforms would be a huge endeavor for a project like Numba, so a simpler alternative would be great to have. While exploring taichi I discovered that they support multiple "backends", and one of them were OpenGL/Vulkan. While the multiple backends enabled to write one kernel, which could be executed onto multiple platforms, I was more surprised to see OpenGL/Vulkan support, which meant I was kinda platform agnostic, as long as the target platform could setup/run OpenGL/Vulkan. Since OpenGL is a bit older, I was wondering how hard it would be to support Vulkan as a backend for Numba. While the performance would not be on par as using native APIs/frameworks, it would still be a huge benefit and make using different hardware much easier! There has been a comment regarding using the Vulkan LLVM as an intermediate step for Apples Metal API: https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/5706#issuecomment-985233765 I have no experience in such matters, but if someone could give me some hints where to lookup stuff, I could maybe start with a proof of concept!

title: [QST] How does cudf perform groupby and aggregation on uint128 types?
issue_body_excerpt: How does cudf perform groupby and aggregation on uint128 types?
comments_excerpt: cuDF only supports 128 bit types for decimal (fixed point) data. Generic 128 bit signed/unsigned integer data types are not supported. See this blog post for information about 128 bit decimals, which are internally represented by the CUDA extension type `__int128`: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/implementing-high-precision-decimal-arithmetic-with-cuda-int128/ @bdice Is there a plan to support it in the future? "128 bit types for decimal" cannot be used for the group by column. Is there any other solution? Currently I don’t think there is a plan for supporting 128 bit integer types. The cost to extend the type matrix is very high due to compile time, and there are a lot of places where 64 bit integers are the maximum width we could support for computation without significant changes to the library’s internals. How is your input data being stored / computed? (Where do the 128 bit types come from?) Do you need this for cuDF Python or some other interface? Side note: I did a little more research and I think the CUDA extended types may only include signed `__int128`. I didn’t see any references to unsigned `__uint128`, so it is unlikely that cuDF could support the unsigned type without new CUDA language features. @bdice The uint128 data comes from the hash calculation of character strings, which improves the GPU computing performance and uses 128 bits to ensure a very low collision probability. Since you don't have to do math on these hash values, you just need to store them, you have some decent options: - You could use a string column with a UTF-8 encoding of the raw binary data (or a plain string encoding of the hexadecimal or decimal integer form of the value, if you wished) - You could use two uint64s in a struct column - You could use two uint64s in a list column...

title: Discussion on multi-GPU support for cuFFT and cuSOLVER
issue_body_excerpt: Original context: See #2644. Some of CUDA libraries like cuFFT and cuSOLVER provide native multi-GPU support. However, there is no guarantee that multiple GPUs will outperform single GPU; on the contrary, for cuFFT I found in https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/2644#issuecomment-558835428 that any workload that can be handled in one GPU should ***not*** be processed using multi GPUs; the extra data transfer just kills the performance (even if NVLinks are present). I suspect the same holds for cuSOLVER. Since CuPy operations incurs additional memory overhead, I think it is clear that multi-GPU is useful only when the workload is too large to fit in one GPU. For such excessive workloads, it's better/unavoidable to start from NumPy arrays directly, such as the "NumPy-in, NumPy-out" feature currently implemented in #2644. **This thread is for discussions regarding this feature and other possible alternative strategies.**
